title: Introducing Nexus 1.0
summary: Nexus is the agentic harness behind Pylon's agents: the context, memory, routing, and guardrails that turn model reasoning into production support work.
body_markdown:
Frontier models are increasingly capable of reasoning, searching, using tools, and working through complex problems.


But a real support issue asks for more than a capable model. An agent needs to know which customer it's working with, how that customer uses and has configured the product, what's changed, where to find evidence, which tools it can use, what actions it's allowed to take, and when it should stop or ask for approval.


[Nexus](https://www.usepylon.com/nexus) is the harness behind Pylon's agents. It's what turns model reasoning into production support work.


## The model is only one part of the system


Any team can use the same models that power Pylon. What they don't get automatically is the rest of what the work demands. A single investigation may span customer history, logs, documentation, code, and internal systems. The agent has to find the right evidence across those sources, keep track of where the investigation stands, and decide what to do next.


The model provides the reasoning. Nexus provides the system around it.


## How Nexus fits into Pylon


Pylon builds three layers of intelligence from the data you connect: Support Intelligence, Account Intelligence, and Product Intelligence.


Those layers organize what Pylon knows about your support operation, your customers, and your product. Nexus decides how agents use that context to investigate, resolve, coordinate, and act.


Support Intelligence includes prior resolutions, escalation policies, active incidents, channel preferences, tone, and support processes.


Account Intelligence includes the customer's use case, implementation details, stakeholders, usage, sentiment, contract details, and account-specific constraints.


Product Intelligence includes documentation, bugs, feature requests, roadmap context, code, engineering discussions, logs, and releases.


Nexus puts that intelligence to work through six connected mechanisms: context, memory, traces, routing, guardrails, and continuous improvement.


Here's what that looks like for one support request.


## What happens during an investigation


Take a customer who reports that a field isn't syncing correctly with their CRM.


Here's what happens between that request arriving and an agent taking action.


### 1. Construct the current state


Before the agent starts investigating, Nexus rebuilds what has happened since it last acted.


The customer has sent a video of the sync error and followed up with another message. Nexus transcribes the video, adds the new reply to the session, and brings in work that has already happened in the background, including a classification of the issue as a CRM integration problem.


The agent begins with the current state of the issue instead of piecing it together from scratch.


### 2. Load the right context


Next, Nexus determines what the agent needs for this investigation.


It pulls Support Intelligence from similar investigations and active incidents, Account Intelligence about the customer's CRM use case and sync requirements, and Product Intelligence from documentation and open feature requests.


It also loads the relevant Skills, memory, guidance, permissions, and tools.


The goal isn't to give the model everything Pylon knows, but to give it the information and capabilities that matter for the work in front of it.


### 3. Investigate and adapt


The agent starts working through the issue.


It checks for an active incident, searches the logs, looks up the error in Salesforce docs, and compares its findings with the code and product roadmap. Nexus routes each step to the model best suited to the task, and each result returns as a structured observation the agent can use to choose its next move.


Not every path is useful. A knowledge base search leads to a dead end, so the agent moves on. Each useful result becomes new evidence.


In this case, the logs point to an invalid field type. Salesforce docs identify the field as a multi-select picklist, and the code confirms there is no handler for it. The investigation ends with a specific conclusion: the customer's field type isn't supported for sync.


### 4. Guard the outcome


Reaching a conclusion doesn't automatically mean the agent can take every action that follows from it.


Nexus checks the output against the controls configured for the agent. In this example, the customer-facing response is checked for PII, sender identity, and citations before it can be sent.


The same investigation also surfaces a possible feature request. That write action requires human approval, so it's held rather than executed automatically.


### 5. Learn from the run


The investigation doesn't disappear when it's over.


Nexus stores the trace, including what the agent searched, which tools it used, where it hit dead ends, what evidence it found, and how the run ended.


Those traces can surface things that should change. In this example, the investigation identifies a gap in the CRM documentation and produces a new evaluation case. The approved feature request can also be associated with the customer account.


That case can then be used to test future changes.


## What happens when a better model comes out?


Different tasks have different requirements for reasoning quality, latency, cost, and control. The best model for one step in an investigation may not be the best model for another, and those tradeoffs change as new models become available.


Nexus separates everything support-specific from the model itself. Pylon can evaluate new models and techniques against the work its agents actually do, change routing when a configuration performs better, and keep the surrounding context, tools, permissions, and workflows intact. As models improve, Nexus can take advantage of those gains without being rebuilt.


We maintain eval sets for different classes of support work and rerun them whenever we test a change, whether that's better retrieval, more useful memory, different routing, or a new model. A change ships only when it shows a measurable improvement in quality, cost, or latency.


Nexus 1.0 is what powers Pylon's agents today. We'll keep sharing what changes.
